traumatic_stressor_required.name: Traumatic Event
traumatic_stressor_required.description: Exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence.

types.Witnessing: Witnessing, in person, the event(s) as it occurred to others.
types.Indirect Exposure (Learning): Learning that the traumatic event(s) occurred to a close family member or close friend. (Note: Violent or accidental).
types.Repeated Exposure to Aversive Details: Experiencing repeated or extreme exposure to aversive details of the traumatic event(s) (e.g., first responders collecting human remains; excludes exposure through media).

examples.Combat and War: War, combat, or experience as a prisoner of war.
examples.Physical Violence: Physical assault, mugging, kidnapping, terrorism, or domestic violence.
examples.Sexual Violence: Rape, sexual assault, or sexual abuse.
examples.Accidents: Severe traffic accidents, industrial accidents, or fire.
examples.Natural Disasters: Natural disasters such as earthquakes or floods.
examples.Medical Trauma: Life-threatening medical situations such as waking up during surgery.

psychosocial_stressor_required.name: Psychosocial Stressor
psychosocial_stressor_required.description: Identifiable life events that cause psychological distress but do not reach the level of life-threatening trauma

examples.Relational: Breakup, divorce, marital conflict, family conflict, or interpersonal problems.
examples.Occupational: Termination, job loss, workplace bullying, excessive workload, or retirement.
examples.Academic: Academic failure, entrance exam failure, transferring schools, or school maladjustment.
examples.Economic: Bankruptcy, debt, sudden drop in economic status, or poverty.
examples.Health: Diagnosis of a chronic illness, surgery recovery, or infertility.
examples.Developmental: Life cycle changes such as independence, marriage, childbirth, or menopause.
